content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes BestowGNN, a stacking framework that supports graph-aware propagation. This framework employs techniques including bagging, model ensemble, and stacking by the usage of the AutoGluon package. For the stack ensemble, they closely follow the methodology of AutoGluon. For the selected baselines, they achieve comparable or competitive results on several datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Weaknesses
1. This paper is hard to read. The writing of this paper is bad. The logic of this paper is unclear and hard to follow. 
2. The experimental part is not convincing and some SOTA methods are missing. For example, for Reddit, a not recent the state of the art method is JKNet + DropEdge by [1], which is a work accepted by ICLR 2020, with a testing accuracy of 97.02. There are also many recent works that can achieve higher than 97% on Reddit. Additionally, for OGB-Products, the state-of-the-art method last year (2021 Dec) is GIANT-XRT+SAGN+MCR+C&S with a test accuracy of 86.73 but this method is not included. For the OGB-Arvix, the state-of-the-art method for Jan 2022 is GIANT-XRT+DRGAT+KD with a test accuracy of 76.33. The claim that they achieve the state of the art performances is misleading.
Also, the model size of BestowGNN is not shared and the comparison may be not fair. 
3. The novelty of the proposed method is low. The core implementations are borrowed from the AutoGluon package.
4. The detailed illustration of network design is missing and can not be inferred from figure 1.



References:

[1] 'DropEdge: Towards Deep Graph Convolutional Networks on Node Classification' ICLR 2020 by Rong et al.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity** : very low and hard to understand. 

**Quality** : low.

**Originality**: fair.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, because of the concerns listed in the above weaknesses, I vote for the rejection of this paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work focuses on investigating how to adapt ML pipelines designed for supervised learning to node classification/regression tasks with graph-structured data. Then, the authors propose a framework of stack ensembling with graph propagation called BestowGNN for Bagged, Ensembled, Stacked Training Of Well-balanced GNNs. To address the potential shortcoming of label leakage, they also formalize how their bagging and stacking framework can effectively mitigate the label leakage issue within the 
graph setting using analytical tools from differential privacy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1.The paper is well-written and easy to follow.

2.The developed method is promising to boost the performance by stacking existing GNNs.


Weakness:

1.The description of the developed method can be improved, especially the notation.

2.The novelty is limited and almost all of detailed techniques used are already existing.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The notation should be improved

1.the notation k is reused in k-fold (A.1) and kth iteration in Eq. (4)

2.Compute F^(t) using Eq. (4), but F^(t) does not even appear in Sec 3.3

3.A suggestion to modify the notation in the loop of A.1 from 
for i to n to for n to N, and 
for j to k to for k to K, which will be more straightforward for readers to understand.

The novelty of this work is limited.
The main contribution of this work have been listed in the pipeline shown in Fig. 1, which does not provides any novel technique in the aspect of bagging or ensemble methods. Moreover, there is also no modification in the updating equation of graph-aware 
propagation as shown in Eq.(1), where the second term is a widely-used Laplacian regularization.

Experiments

1.No description of hyperparameter selection.

2.For the results of ablation study in Table.4, it can only demonstrate bagging can effectively boost the model performance and outperform no-bagging methods, rather than proving that this gain is from mitigation of label leakage and over-fitting issues. It will be more convincing to design an ablation study to measure the degree of label leakage to demonstrate bagging can reduce the degree of label leakage.

Additional questions

1.It is still not clear to me why the previous SAGN and GAMLP suffer from the risk of label leakage, even they have claimed their methods can effectively alleviate label leakage.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a unified framework which incorporates stacking-based ensemble learning into graph-based learning, i.e., learning in the non-IID setting. It treats models trained on node features in the IID setting as base models, and performs graph-based propagation to generate features for the following stacking layers. The authors provide theoretical analysis for the framework's ability in mitigating the label leakage.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
- The idea of incorporating stacking-based ensemble learning into graph-based learning seems novel.
- The authors provide theoretical anlaysis for the label leakage problem.

Cons:
- The proposed framework is not quite convincing. The authors fail to justify why they choose the simple graph propagation, rather than graph convolution, to generate non-IID features. Some closely related work, e.g., BertGCN, is not compared in experiments. Moreover, there is only a simple ensemble based method (Ensemble GCN). It is not fair to compare ensemble method with non-ensemble baselines.
- The presentation needs significant improvements. Moreover, the derivation seems problematic, and necessary details are missing (please see the next item for details).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Althought the idea of incorporating stacking-based ensemble learning into graph-based learning could be novel, there are also a number of major problems in terms of clarity, quality and reproducibility:
(1) Algorithm 1 seems problematic. The first loop variable l, never appear in the body of the loop. It is not known how the multiple layers of stacking are constructed.
(2) How does each base model's input look like? Do you take the labels as input, and how? How do you split labeled and unlabled data? These necessary details are missing. The notations are often used casually. For example, both Eq.(6) and Eq.(7) sum over the same Y, which is defined to be the predictions for chunk j (should be containing both labeled and unlabeled nodes).
(3) The theoretical analysis could be problematic. Firstly, Eq.(8) of definition 1 does not contain the varible x in the expectation. How is this expectation computed? Second, how do you obtain Eqs.(9) and (10) in Prelimianry 1 of the appendix? The update equation (4) contain hyperparameter alpha and lambda. Why are they missing? Furthermore, the update should also take the initial prediction of the node into consideration. However, it is also missing in (9) and (10). Thirdly, it is easy to understand function "f" in proposition 3 denote the prediciton function, and f(x;D) denote the prediction of x based on dataset D (although the authors do not explicitly explain it). However, what is the meaning of f(D)? And |f|? What is sensitivity of f? Finally, in the proof for theorem 1, how do you derive m(x;theta(D))=m(x*theta(D))? What is MLP assumption? Is your base model always a MLP? All the above problems hinder the understanding (and checking the correctness) of the theoretical analysis. I don't list all the problems. There are also other presentation issues.
(4) Some statements in the technical part could be problematic. For example, (a) in section 4.2, "allow stacker models to access the original node features X by concatenating X with the base model's predictions". How do you concatenate, for example, text, with predicted probabilities? "Our stacker models are simply chosen as the same types of models as the base models". This is inconsistent with algorithm 1, where a simple weighted combination is adopted as the stacking function; (b) in section 4.4, "the propagation of base model predictions across the graph implies label information is shared across the k-fold chunks used to hold-out some nodes from some models". Why does the propagation of predictions across the graph among nodes lead to label sharing? (c) the first sentence of section 5.  Label utilization is not necessarily connected to input features.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the idea incorporating stacking-based ensemble learning into graph-based learning could be novel, there are a number of major issues: (1) the proposed solution is not well justified and necessary baselines are missing; (2) the paper is hard to follow and there are a lot of problematic contents, which make it difficult to evaluate the correctness of the theoretical analysis. Consequently, the reproducibility could also be a problem.

content.title: A Robust Stacking Framework for Training Deep Graph Models with Multifaceted Node Features
content.abstract:
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with numerical node features and graph structure as inputs have demonstrated superior performance on various supervised learning tasks with graph data. However the numerical node features utilized by GNNs are commonly extracted from raw data which is of text or tabular (numeric/categorical) type in most real-world applications. 
The best models for such data types in most standard supervised learning settings with IID (non-graph) data are not simple neural network layers and thus are not easily incorporated into a GNN. Here we propose a robust stacking framework that fuses graph-aware propagation with arbitrary models intended for IID data, which are ensembled and stacked in multiple layers. Our layer-wise framework leverages bagging and stacking strategies to enjoy strong generalization, in a manner which effectively mitigates label leakage and overfitting. Across a variety of graph datasets with tabular/text node features, our method achieves comparable or superior performance relative to both tabular/text and graph neural network models, as well as existing state-of-the-art hybrid strategies that combine the two.
